seoDescription: Learn how to install and run the Automatic1111 Stable Diffusion Web UI on your Apple Silicon Mac, including M1 and M2 devices. This comprehensive guide walks you through the entire setup process, from installing prerequisites like Homebrew, Python, and Git, to cloning the repository and downloading the necessary models. Discover how to launch the Web UI, generate your first images, and apply command-line arguments like --med-vram and --opt-attention to optimize performance and manage VRAM usage on your Mac.

summary:
## Prerequisites

Before installing the Stable Diffusion Web UI, you must have **Homebrew** installed. You can install or update it by running the command from [brew.sh](https://brew.sh).

Once Homebrew is ready, install the required packages using the Terminal:

> [!NOTE]
> `brew install cmake protobuf rust python@3.10 git wget`

## Installation Steps

1.  **Clone the Repository**: Open a Terminal and run the `git clone` command with the URL for the [AUTOMATIC1111/stable-diffusion-webui](https://github.com/AUTOMATIC1111/stable-diffusion-webui) repository.
    
    `git clone https://github.com/AUTOMATIC1111/stable-diffusion-webui.git`
    
2.  **Download a Model**: Download a Stable Diffusion model checkpoint (e.g., v1.5 from Hugging Face). These are large files, typically several gigabytes.
    
3.  **Place the Model**: Move the downloaded checkpoint file (`.ckpt` or `.safetensors`) into the `stable-diffusion-webui/models/Stable-diffusion/` directory.

## Running the Web UI

_To launch the application for the first time and in the future:_ 

1.  Open a Terminal.
2.  Navigate to the project directory: `cd stable-diffusion-webui`
3.  Execute the launch script: `./webui.sh`

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The first launch will take a significant amount of time as it downloads and installs dependencies like PyTorch, GFPGAN, and CodeFormer.

Once it's running, open the local URL (e.g., `http://127.0.0.1:7860`) in your browser to access the interface.

## Performance Optimization

You can add command-line arguments to the `webui-user.sh` file to manage resource usage and troubleshoot problems. Uncomment the `export COMMANDLINE_ARGS=""` line and add flags inside the quotes.

**Common flags:**

*   `--med-vram`: Reduces VRAM usage at a slight performance cost. Recommended for systems with less VRAM.
*   `--low-vram`: Further reduces VRAM usage for low-memory systems.
*   `--opt-attention`: An optimization that can improve performance.
*   `--skip-torch-cuda-test`: Skips the CUDA test, which can help if the startup fails.
*   `--no-half`: Disables half-precision calculations, can fix black-screen issues but is slower.
*   `--use-cpu all`: Forces the use of the CPU for all tasks, which will be very slow but can bypass GPU-related issues.

## Important Considerations

*   **Performance**: Performance on Apple Silicon (M1/M2) is significantly slower than on a PC with a dedicated high-end **Nvidia GPU**.
*   **Compatibility**: Some features like **training** or the **CLIP Interrogator** may not work correctly on all Mac setups.
*   **Hardware Matters**: Performance scales with your hardware. An M2 Max will perform better than an M1 Air.
transcription:
## Introduction & Mac Performance Caveats

What's up? I'm Troubleshoot, welcome back to another video. In this quick guide, I'll be showing you how to get Automatic1111's Stable Diffusion web UI running on a Mac. Obviously, this isn't going to give you the highest performance. On an M1 or M2 chip, you're going to get the best performance on a desktop PC with a powerful Nvidia graphics card. If you're running a Hackintosh or something along those lines, this will probably work out great for you though.

This is something built for Linux or Windows, so even though it can run, you are probably able to squeeze out much better performance using better hardware and a better setup. Anyways, without further ado, how do we get this set up and working on a Mac?

## Installing & Updating Homebrew

Well, over here I'm connected to an M1 MacBook Air and I'll be showing you how you can set it up. First of all, we'll need Homebrew installed. If you don't already have it installed, open up a browser, head across to brew.sh, and copy this command here. When you've clicked the copy button, open up a new terminal, paste it in, and hit enter.

This will go ahead and install Homebrew after you confirm your password. There we go. So enter, and now we just simply need to wait for this to finish. If you've already installed Homebrew you can run this command again to update it, which is exactly what I'm doing here. There we go, it's now done installing.

## Installing Dependencies with Homebrew

The next step is installing the required programs for this to work. Brew install cmake, protobuf, rust, python at 3.10, git, and wget. I'll hit enter to install all of these bits of software. If you're prompted to hit enter to continue, just make sure to do so. There we go, the download's now complete. I can clear, and we'll run the next command.

## Cloning the Automatic1111 Repository

git clone space followed by the Automatic1111 Stable Diffusion Web UI GitHub URL. You can either Google for Automatic1111 and click the GitHub link or copy the link in the description down below. I'll copy this one here, then I'll paste it in here. So, git clone the git URL, hit enter, and it'll download the project onto our PC so we can run it in just a moment.

If we type in `open .`, we'll open the folder in a Finder window, and inside of here, you'll find stable-diffusion-webui. Sweet. I'll open up this folder, sort by kind, and now we're back in a similar looking folder structure that we have on Windows.

## Downloading & Placing the Model Checkpoint

What we need to do here is open the models folder over here, then stable-diffusion, and inside of here we need to drop Stable Diffusion checkpoints or safetensor files. These are models that will actually be used to generate images. For this, the easiest place to download them is probably Hugging Face if you want the original ones, but there are other websites that allow you to download modified and pre-tuned Stable Diffusion models. I won't go into that here though.

I'll download Stable Diffusion 1.5 from Hugging Face. Obviously you can get version 2, I think there's even 2.1 now. For me, 1.5 is what I'll be using. I'll head across to files and versions, then scroll down and locate the checkpoint, which you can see there are two of them here. I'll download 1.5 pruned and click the small download file button next to this here, and it'll start downloading the file. When this is done downloading, simply move it into this stable-diffusion folder here.

Obviously this is where most of your space will be used up when you're using Stable Diffusion for image generation. It's mostly the models and things like that. When you do start up Stable Diffusion, there'll be a further two or so gigabytes downloaded and installed, which is PyTorch and other Python libraries for setting up the image generation software. 7.1, 7.2, there we go. I'll drag it into this stable-diffusion-models folder. Awesome.

## First Launch & Dependency Installation

What we'll do now is minimize our file browser and head back to our terminal that we still haven't closed. And I'll type in `cd st` hit tab to automatically type out the rest of it, in this case `stable-diffusion-webui`. I'll hit enter and now we're inside of the Stable Fusion web UI folder we were just looking at. Inside of here we have `webui-user.sh` where we can set up options and things like that for Stable Diffusion, and we have `webui.sh` that we can use to start up the Automatic1111 Stable Diffusion Web UI.

So in order to just run it straight out the bat and install things as necessary, run `./web` hit tab to type in `webui.sh`. Or simply type it out yourself. Tab just automatically tries to guess what you're typing out and fills out the rest of it. If you get the wrong file, just keep hitting tab and it should cycle through them, but I'll just give you an option in this case anyways. Hitting enter for `./webui.sh`, it'll start up the Python installer and things like that to install all the necessary packages.

It's downloading 50 megs here, two gigs there, back and forth. Well, never mind. It seems like it didn't need to download two gigs of PyTorch; it's actually a lot smaller. That's pretty good. We'll have to see how the performance is though. I don't expect anything groundbreaking, but we'll see. After it's prepared the necessary packages, it'll go ahead and install gfpgan, code former, and things like that, which are all different packages and projects used in this greater project, Stable Diffusion. This could take a few minutes to a handful of minutes depending on the speed of your internet.

Once it's installed, it'll eventually start up. You'll see an HTTP link here. Simply right-click, copy this, and head across there in a browser.

## Generating Your First Image

When you navigate there, you'll see this familiar Web UI. Obviously, you can customize things as you please. I'll just type, say, 'pool' maybe, and generate. The first time you generate, this will probably take a lot longer than the other times. And if we have a look at the console over here, you'll see exactly what it's doing as it's working. Obviously, it'll be quite slow, but you can still use it and it's great to see that it is working. There's a few optimizations to make it a bit better, which I'll get to in just a moment.

And there we go. After 20 iterations and a few seconds, there is a 512x512 image of a pool. It's a heck of a lot slower than using a dedicated graphics card, but it works, and it's amazing. There's only a few caveats to running this on Mac. For some people, training won't work, the CLIP interrogator may not work for other people.

## Optimizing Performance with Command-Line Arguments

Now, of course, this is a cheaper MacBook Air M1, but assuming you're running into issues with VRAM, trying to make bigger pictures or generate with a higher batch size than one, there are a few optimizations that we can try to get this to run a bit faster. If I pull across the console here, it reached 2.7 iterations per second and it took 50 seconds or so to generate an image. But we can try and improve it. I'll hit Ctrl+C to cancel out of this.

And inside of this folder, we have a `webui-user.sh` file. I'll navigate back to here either with `open .` to open it in Finder or reopening the Finder window we had opened previously. And I'll scroll down to `webui-user.sh`. I'll right-click, open with, and choose a text editor. Inside, if you look for the line `COMMANDLINE_ARGS` and you'll remove the hash at the start of it, allowing us to type in here some commands that may help performance are `--med-vram` as such, which should load the model and things like that in parts into RAM, giving you better RAM usage while you're using it and better performance, hopefully.

Another suggested option is `opt-attention`. I'll be copying this with Command+C and pasting with Command+V as that's also a pretty good option to have. If you're still experiencing issues, you can run it with `low-vram` as well, instead of just `med-vram`. If you find that you're getting issues launching it at all, some of the command line options that you can try and add are `--skip-torch-cuda-test` as such, and `no-half` as well, as `use-cpu all` to try and use CPU only. This could help save you if you're having issues on your Mac. Use Command+S to save. We can leave this open or whatever.

## How to Relaunch & Final Thoughts

And we'll be opening a terminal in this folder here. So in future to start it up, just open a terminal, use `cd` space and type in `st` for stable diffusion, hit tab to type out the whole thing, enter to navigate into it, and then `./webui.sh`. It should then start up and work properly as per before. Of course, some of these options will lower your performance even further, but if you have to use some of them, then you have to use some of them. There we go, now it's loaded. I can reopen it in Firefox, tell it to generate a new image, and just like that it'll start iterating through once more.

So your performance will really vary on the kind of hardware that you have, whether it's an M1 or M2, an Air, a Pro, a Max, or whatever. The better hardware you have, the more money you spend on it, but the better performance you should get in Stable Diffusion web UI. Now obviously I wouldn't recommend running this on a Mac and getting a Mac just to run Stable Diffusion web UI, as with a proper Nvidia graphics card on a desktop you can get much, much better performance. But for now, it is what it is, and with that comes the end of this super quick video.

Of course, you can play around with commands that go in here to further customize your install and hopefully getting it to work a bit better, but that really just comes down to your system and playing around with it. That's the basic install for Automatic1111's Stable Diffusion web UI. You now know how to download it, open it, generate images, and open it in the future after installing it. So hopefully you found this video really useful. Thank you all for watching. My name's been Troubleshoot, and I'll see you all next time. Ciao.
